claim: Individual malaria infections can carry multiple strains of Plasmodium falciparum with varying levels of relatedness.
source: Individual malaria infections can carry multiple strains of Plasmodium falciparum with varying levels of relatedness.
evidence: This is a statement in the abstract that is supported by the data and analysis presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The rate of mixed infection varies from 29% to 63% across countries in the Pf3k dataset.
source: we find that the rate of mixed infection varies from 29% to 63% across countries
evidence: This claim is supported by the deconvolution analysis of 2344 field samples using DEploidIBD.

claim: 51% of mixed infections involve more than two strains.
source: 51% of mixed infections involve more than two strains
evidence: This is derived from the analysis of the Pf3k dataset showing the distribution of K=2, K=3, and K=4 infections.

claim: 47% of symptomatic dual infections contain sibling strains likely to have been co-transmitted from a single mosquito.
source: we estimate that 47% of symptomatic dual infections contain sibling strains likely to have been co-transmitted from a single mosquito
evidence: This estimate is based on the classification of K=2 mixed infections using simulated IBD distributions from pf-meiosis.

claim: Prevalence correlates within Africa, but not Asia, with both the rate of mixed infection and the level of IBD.
source: we find that prevalence correlates within Africa, but not Asia, with both the rate of mixed infection and the level of IBD
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis between PfPR estimates from the Malaria Atlas Project and mixed infection statistics.

claim: Mixed infections are common in regions of Africa with high rates of prevalence.
source: Such mixed infections, also known as complex infections, are likely indicative of intense local exposure rates, being common in regions of Africa with high rates of prevalence (Howes et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by Howes et al., 2016.

claim: Mixed infections have been documented for P. vivax and other malaria-causing parasites even in regions of much lower prevalence.
source: However, they have also been documented for P. vivax and other malaria-causing parasites (Mueller et al., 2007; Collins, 2012), even in regions of much lower prevalence (Howes et al., 2016; Steenkeste et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Mixed infections have been associated with increased disease severity.
source: Mixed infections have been associated with increased disease severity (de Roode et al., 2005)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to de Roode et al., 2005.

claim: Mixed infections facilitate the generation of genomic diversity within the parasite, enabling co-transmission to the mosquito vector where sexual recombination occurs.
source: and also facilitate the generation of genomic diversity within the parasite, enabling co-transmission to the mosquito vector where sexual recombination occurs (Mzilahowa et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Mzilahowa et al., 2007.

claim: Genome sequencing provides a more powerful approach for detecting mixed infections than genetic barcodes.
source: Although mixed infections can be studied from genetic barcodes (Galinsky et al., 2015), genome sequencing provides a more powerful approach for detecting mixed infections (O'Brien et al., 2016; Chang et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies comparing methods.

claim: 58% of P. vivax mixed infections show long stretches of within host homozygosity.
source: For example, in P. vivax, 58% of mixed infections show long stretches of within host homozygosity (Pearson et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Pearson et al., 2016.

claim: P. falciparum shows an average of 78.7% allele sharing in Malawi and 87.6% sharing in Thailand.
source: In addition, (Nkhoma et al., 2012) reported an average of 78.7% P. falciparum allele sharing in Malawi and 87.6% sharing in Thailand.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Nkhoma et al., 2012.

claim: Existing deconvolution methods assume equal relatedness along the genome, which can lead to errors when strains are siblings.
source: Because existing deconvolution methods assume equal relatedness along the genome, differences in relatedness that occur, for example through infection by sibling strains, can lead to errors in the estimation of the number, proportions and sequences of individual strains (Figure 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the description of limitations in existing methods and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: DEploidIBD separates estimation of strain number, proportions, and relatedness from the problem of inferring genome sequences.
source: The method separates estimation of strain number, proportions, and relatedness (specifically the identity-by-descent, or IBD, profile along the genome) from the problem of inferring genome sequences.
evidence: This is a description of the methodological approach taken in DEploidIBD.

claim: DEploidIBD was applied to 2344 field isolates of P. falciparum collected from 13 countries over a range of years (2001–2014).
source: We apply DEploidIBD to 2344 field isolates of P. falciparum collected from 13 countries over a range of years (2001–2014) and available through the Pf3k Project (see Appendix)
evidence: This describes the dataset analyzed in the study.

claim: Nearly half of symptomatic mixed infections arise from the transmission of sibling strains.
source: estimating that nearly half of symptomatic mixed infections arise from the transmission of sibling strains
evidence: This is based on the classification analysis using pf-meiosis simulations.

claim: There is evidence of mixed infections propagated through multiple cycles of host-vector transmission.
source: as well as demonstrating the propagation of mixed infections through multiple cycles of host-vector transmission
evidence: This is inferred from the presence of M>1 classifications in the data.

claim: Regional rates of mixed infection and levels of background IBD are correlated with estimates of malaria parasite prevalence at a global level.
source: showing that, at a global level, regional rates of mixed infection and levels of background IBD are correlated with estimates of malaria parasite prevalence
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis with MAP prevalence data.

claim: For two strains, there are two possible IBD states (IBD or non-IBD).
source: Thus, for two strains, there are two possible IBD states (IBD or non-IBD)
evidence: This is a mathematical statement about the number of IBD configurations.

claim: For three strains there are five IBD states (all IBD, none IBD and the three pairwise IBD configurations).
source: for three strains there are five states (all IBD, none IBD and the three pairwise IBD configurations)
evidence: This is a mathematical statement about the number of IBD configurations.

claim: For four strains there are fifteen IBD states.
source: for four strains there are fifteen states (see Appendix)
evidence: This is a mathematical statement about the number of IBD configurations.

claim: DEploid and DEploidIBD performed comparably on experimentally generated mixed infections, except in the case of three strains with equal proportions where DEploid performed better.
source: Using this approach, we found that DEploid and DEploidIBD performed comparably, except in the case of three strains with equal proportions, where LD information is necessary to achieve accurate deconvolution and DEploid performed better.
evidence: This is based on validation using 27 experimentally generated mixed infections.

claim: Both DEploid and DEploidIBD struggled to deconvolute in silico mixtures of four strains, typically underestimating the number of strains present.
source: Both DEploid and DEploidIBD struggled to deconvolute our in silico mixtures of four strains, typically underestimating the number of strains present.
evidence: This is based on validation using in silico mixtures of laboratory strains.

claim: For mixtures of two strains, both DEploid and DEploidIBD performed well in scenarios where the IBD between strains was low (<=25%).
source: For mixtures of two strains, both DEploid and DEploidIBD performed well in scenarios where the IBD between strains was low (<=25%).
evidence: This is based on validation using in silico field mixtures.

claim: DEploidIBD tended to estimate more IBD than was simulated in Asian samples, likely reflecting the presence of higher background IBD in Asia.
source: In Asia, DEploidIBD tended to estimate more IBD than was simulated (Figure 2B). However, this likely reflects the presence of higher background IBD in Asia rather than systematic error.
evidence: This is based on validation using in silico field mixtures and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: DEploidIBD consistently gave the correct number of strains and proportions in K=3 mixed infections with imbalanced proportions, as long as the median coverage was > 20x.
source: In contrast, DEploidIBD consistently gave the correct number of strains and proportions in such cases, and produced IBD statistics that were accurate as long as the median coverage of simulated infections was > 20x.
evidence: This is based on validation using in silico field mixtures of K=3 strains.

claim: Both methods struggled to deconvolute mixed infections of four strains.
source: Both methods struggled to deconvolute mixed infections of four strains (Figure 2—figure supplement 2)
evidence: This is based on validation using in silico field mixtures of K=4 strains.

claim: Rates of genotype error are similar for DEploid and DEploidIBD in settings of low relatedness.
source: We compared the haplotype inferences between DEploid and DEpoloidIBD using the error model described in the Appendix, and found that rates of genotype error are similar for the two approaches in settings of low relatedness (DEploidIBD has an error rate of 0.7% per site per strain for 20/80 mixtures and 1.4% for 50/50 mixtures).
evidence: This is based on haplotype quality analysis of in silico K=2 infections.

claim: For 20/80% mixtures with high relatedness, genotype error for DEploid increased to 1.8%, while remaining at 0.8% for DEploidIBD.
source: However, for the 20/80% mixtures with high relatedness, genotype error for DEploid increased to 1.8%, while remaining at 0.8% for DEploidIBD (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is based on haplotype quality analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Switch errors in haplotype estimation are comparable between DEploid and DEploidIBD and decrease with increasing relatedness due to higher homozygosity.
source: Switch errors in haplotype estimation are comparable between the two methods and decrease with increasing relatedness due to higher homozygosity (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is based on haplotype quality analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Within Africa, rates of mixed infection vary from 29% in The Gambia to 63% in Malawi.
source: Within Africa, rates of mixed infection vary from 29% in The Gambia to 63% in Malawi (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is based on the application of DEploidIBD to the Pf3k dataset and shown in Figure 4A.

claim: In Southeast Asian samples, mixed infection rates vary from 21% in Thailand to 54% in Bangladesh.
source: In Southeast Asian samples, mixed infection rates are in general lower, though also vary considerably; from 21% in Thailand to 54% in Bangladesh.
evidence: This is based on the application of DEploidIBD to the Pf3k dataset.

claim: Between 5.1% (Senegal) and 40% (Malawi) of individuals have infections carrying more than two strains.
source: We observe that between 5.1% (Senegal) and 40% (Malawi) of individuals have infections carrying more than two strains.
evidence: This is based on the application of DEploidIBD to the Pf3k dataset.

claim: In dual infections, the average fraction of the genome inferred to be IBD ranges from 14% in Guinea to 65% in West Cambodia.
source: In dual infections, the average fraction of the genome inferred to be IBD ranges from 14% in Guinea to 65% in West Cambodia (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is based on the application of DEploidIBD to the Pf3k dataset and shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Asian populations show, on average, a higher level of relatedness within dual infections (44%) compared to African populations (26%).
source: Asian populations show, on average, a higher level of relatedness within dual infections (44%) compared to African populations ( 26%).
evidence: This is based on the application of DEploidIBD to the Pf3k dataset.

claim: Levels of IBD in samples with three or more strains are comparable to those seen in dual infections (average IBD being 45% in Asia and 37% in Africa).
source: Levels of IBD in samples with three or more strains are comparable to those seen in dual infections (average IBD being 45% in Asia and 37% in Africa)
evidence: This is based on the application of DEploidIBD to the Pf3k dataset.

claim: 51% of all mixed infections involve strains with over 30% of the genome being IBD.
source: Overall, 51% of all mixed infections involve strains with over 30% of the genome being IBD.
evidence: This is based on the application of DEploidIBD to the Pf3k dataset.

claim: Populations with higher rates of mixed infection tend to have lower levels of IBD within mixed infections.
source: We find that populations with higher rates of mixed infection tend to have lower levels of IBD within mixed infections (linear model p=0.06 after accounting for a continental level difference and weighted by sample size).
evidence: This is based on correlation analysis between mixed infection rate and IBD levels.

claim: Conditioning on at least one progeny originating from an outbred oocyst, the expected IBD asymptotically approaches 1/2 as the total number of oocysts grows.
source: Conditioning on at least one progeny originating from an outbred oocyst (such that a detectable recombination event has occurred), the expected IBD asymptotically approaches 1/2 as the total number of oocysts grows (see Appendix).
evidence: This is based on the pf-meiosis simulation framework.

claim: The effective number of strains is uncorrelated with PfPR2-10 across Asia.
source: but is uncorrelated across Asia
evidence: This is based on correlation analysis with MAP prevalence data.

claim: PfPR2-10 is negatively correlated with background IBD across Africa but not in Asia.
source: and across Africa but not in Asia
evidence: This is based on correlation analysis with MAP prevalence data.

claim: Serial co-transmission may occur more readily in low prevalence regions.
source: suggesting that serial co-transmission may occur more readily in low prevalence regions
evidence: This is inferred from the negative correlation between supersibling rate and prevalence.

claim: Field isolates were sequenced to an average read depth of 86 (range 12.6–192.5).
source: Briefly, field isolates were sequenced to an average read depth of 86 (range 12.6–192.5).
evidence: This describes the sequencing coverage of the Pf3k dataset.

claim: After filtering samples for low coverage and cross-species contamination, 2344 samples remained.
source: After filtering samples for low coverage and cross-species contamination, 2344 samples remained.
evidence: This describes the final sample size after quality control.

claim: Samples were grouped into geographical regions by genetic similarity; four in Africa, and three in Asia.
source: For deconvolution, samples were grouped into geographical regions by genetic similarity; four in Africa, and three in Asia. (Table 1).
evidence: This describes the grouping strategy for deconvolution analysis.

claim: The distribution of oocysts in wild-caught Anopheles Gambiae is roughly geometric, with the majority of infected mosquitoes carrying only one oocyst.
source: Studies of wild-caught Anopheles Gambiae suggest that the distribution of oocysts is roughly geometric, with the majority of infected mosquitoes carrying only one oocyst (Beier et al., 1991; Collins et al., 1984).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: A single infected mosquito can undergo multiple meioses in parallel, one occurring for each oocyst that forms on the mosquito midgut.
source: Most importantly, a single infected mosquito can undergo multiple meioses in parallel, one occurring for each oocyst that forms on the mosquito midgut (Ghosh et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ghosh et al., 2000.

claim: In a mosquito infected with two distinct strains, each oocyst can either self (the maternal and paternal strain are the same) or outbreed (the maternal and paternal strains are different).
source: In a mosquito infected with two distinct strains, each oocyst can either self (the maternal and paternal strain are the same) or outbreed (the maternal and paternal strains are different).
evidence: This describes the biological process of meiosis in mosquitoes.

claim: A non-trivial fraction (17%) of all mixed infections had patterns of IBD inconsistent with the simulations.
source: We note that a non-trivial fraction (17%) of all mixed infections had patterns of IBD inconsistent with the simulations (typically with slightly higher IBD levels than background but lower than among siblings).
evidence: This is based on the classification of K=2 mixed infections using pf-meiosis simulations.

claim: 787 samples were identified where low sequencing coverage or the presence of low-frequency strains resulted in unusual haplotypes.
source: We identified 787 samples where low sequencing coverage or the presence of low-frequency strains resulted in unusual haplotypes (see Appendix).
evidence: This describes quality control filtering of haplotypes.

claim: Estimates of strain number, proportions and IBD states from samples with unusual haplotypes are used in subsequent analyses, but not the haplotypes.
source: Estimates of strain number, proportions and IBD states from these samples are used in subsequent analyses, but not the haplotypes.
evidence: This describes how samples with low-quality haplotypes were handled in the analysis.

claim: Senegal samples were screened to contain only one strain by SNP barcode.
source: An important exception are the samples from Senegal which, though collected passively at a clinic, were screened to contain only one strain by SNP barcode (Daniels et al., 2015).
evidence: This describes a specific characteristic of the Senegal samples.

claim: The majority of samples in Pf3k were collected from symptomatic individuals seeking clinical treatment.
source: These samples were collected under a wide range of studies with differing designs, though the majority of samples were collected from symptomatic individuals seeking clinical treatment.
evidence: This describes the sampling design of the Pf3k dataset.

claim: Samples from Senegal have an unusual combination of low mixed infections and also low IBD.
source: However, the continental level effect is driven by Senegal, which has an unusual combination of low mixed infections and also low IBD.
evidence: This is based on the analysis of mixed infection rates and IBD levels across populations.

claim: A recent and dramatic decline in P. falciparum prevalence within Senegal has left an impact on patterns of genetic variation.
source: Previous work has demonstrated how a recent and dramatic decline in P. falciparum prevalence within Senegal has left an impact on patterns of genetic variation (Daniels et al., 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Daniels et al., 2015.

claim: Mixed infection rates are likely to respond rapidly to changes in prevalence.
source: Nevertheless, because mixed infection rates are likely to respond rapidly to changes in prevalence (Volkman et al., 2012)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Volkman et al., 2012.

claim: The amount of IBD expected in a single-bite mixed infection produced from two unrelated parasites strains will always be slightly less than 1/2, and potentially as low as 1/3.
source: Here, we have shown, from first principles, that the amount of IBD expected in a single-bite mixed infection produced from two unrelated parasites strains will always be slightly less than 1/2, and potentially as low as 1/3 (see Appendix).
evidence: This is based on theoretical analysis using the pf-meiosis simulation framework.

claim: Successful establishment of multiple strains through a single infection event is a major source of mixed infection.
source: Firstly, they suggest that successful establishment of multiple strains through a single infection event is a major source of mixed infection.
evidence: This is inferred from the high proportion of sibling infections observed.

claim: The bottlenecks imposed at transmission (to host and vector) are relatively weak.
source: Second, they imply that the bottlenecks imposed at transmission (to host and vector) are relatively weak.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of serial co-transmission.

claim: The differing mechanisms causing mixed infections reflect aspects of local epidemiology.
source: Finally, they indicate that the differing mechanisms causing mixed infections reflect aspects of local epidemiology.
evidence: This is inferred from the geographical variation in mixed infection characteristics.

claim: DEploidIBD infers strain structure in two steps: first estimating the number and proportions of strains, then inferring the individual genomes of the strains.
source: In contrast to our previous work, DEploidIBD infers strain structure in two steps. In the first we estimate the number and proportions of strains using Markov Chain Monte-Carlo (MCMC), allowing for IBD as described above. In the second, we infer the individual genomes of the strains, using the MCMC methodology of , which can account for linkage disequilibrium (LD) between variants, but without updating strain proportions.
evidence: This describes the two-step methodology of DEploidIBD.

claim: DEploidIBD uses a Gamma-Poisson emission model for read counts to account for over-dispersion.
source: To infer IBD states we use a hidden Markov model, which assumes linkage equilibrium between variants for computational efficiency, with a Gamma-Poisson emission model for read counts to account for over-dispersion (see Appendix).
evidence: This describes a technical aspect of the DEploidIBD method.

claim: DEploidIBD limits analysis to a maximum of four strains for computational efficiency.
source: We limit analysis to a maximum of four strains for computational efficiency.
evidence: This describes a limitation of the DEploidIBD method.
